title: Letter Writing
notes: Letter writing is the art of composing written communication to convey information, express feelings, or make requests. In the NEB Class 11 English examination, letter writing is a heavily tested skill, typically carrying 8-12 marks. Students are expected to write two main types of letters: Formal letters (to authorities, editors, principals) and Informal letters (to friends, relatives). Each type has a distinct format, tone, and structure that must be followed precisely.

A formal letter follows a strict format: (1) Sender's address (top left, no date below). (2) Date (below sender's address). (3) Receiver's designation and address (below date). (4) Salutation: 'Sir/Madam' (if name is unknown) or 'Dear Mr. Sharma' (if name is known). (5) Subject: A concise line stating the purpose, preceded by 'Subject:' (e.g., 'Subject: Complaint about irregular water supply'). (6) Body: Three paragraphs — opening (state purpose), middle (explain details), closing (request action/thank). (7) Complimentary close: 'Yours faithfully' (if salutation is 'Sir/Madam') or 'Yours sincerely' (if salutation uses a name). (8) Signature and name.

Formal letters require a respectful, objective, and concise tone. Use formal language: no contractions ('do not' not 'don't'), no slang, no emotional language. Be direct and clear — state the purpose in the first paragraph. Use polite expressions: 'I would like to draw your attention to...', 'I kindly request you to...', 'I would be grateful if...'. Avoid imperative sentences ('Fix the problem now!') — use polite requests instead ('I request you to look into this matter'). Sign off with 'Yours faithfully' (unknown name) or 'Yours sincerely' (known name). The body should be 100-150 words for NEB exams.

Frequently assigned formal letter topics include: (1) Letter to the editor — complaining about a civic issue (garbage disposal, water shortage, traffic, noise pollution). (2) Letter to the principal — requesting permission for an event, complaining about facilities, suggesting improvements. (3) Letter of complaint — to a company about defective products or poor service. (4) Letter of application — applying for a job or scholarship. (5) Letter of enquiry — asking for information about a course, product, or service. For each type, the format remains the same; only the content and specific expressions change.

An informal letter to a friend or relative is less rigid in format but still follows a conventional structure: (1) Sender's address (top right or left). (2) Date. (3) S salutation: 'Dear Ram,' 'Dear Sita,' 'Dear Mama,' 'Dear Bhaija.' (4) Opening: Inquire about the recipient's well-being ('I hope this letter finds you in good health'). (5) Body: Share news, express feelings, ask questions — written in a warm, personal tone. Use contractions ('I'm', 'don't'), exclamations, and casual expressions. (6) Closing: 'Write soon', 'Give my regards to...', 'Love', 'Your friend'. (7) Signature: First name only (e.g., 'Sita'). The body should be 100-120 words for NEB exams.

Informal letters use a warm, personal, and conversational tone. You can use contractions, colloquial expressions, exclamations, and even abbreviations. Express genuine interest in the recipient's life. Share personal news, ask about family, reminisce about shared experiences. Use phrases like: 'How have you been?', 'I can't believe...', 'Guess what happened!', 'I miss you', 'Write back soon'. The key difference from formal letters is the emotional warmth and personal touch. Avoid formal language, rigid structure, or overly polite expressions.

Frequently assigned informal letter topics include: (1) Letter to a friend — inviting them to visit, congratulating on an achievement, sharing news about school/exams, describing a festival. (2) Letter to a relative — congratulating on a birth, wedding, or promotion; expressing sympathy for a loss; sharing family news. (3) Letter of apology — to a friend for missing an event or failing to keep a promise. (4) Letter of thanks — thanking someone for a gift, help, or hospitality. In all cases, the tone should be personal and heartfelt.

The critical differences between formal and informal letters are: (1) Salutation: 'Sir/Madam' (formal) vs. 'Dear Ram' (informal). (2) Subject line: Required in formal letters, omitted in informal. (3) Language: Formal and objective vs. informal and personal. (4) Contractions: Avoided in formal, used in informal. (5) Closing: 'Yours faithfully/sincerely' (formal) vs. 'Love', 'Your friend' (informal). (6) Signature: Full name + designation (formal) vs. first name only (informal). (7) Purpose: Official/business vs. personal/social. Students must identify the letter type from the question and apply the correct format.
confusion: Yours faithfully vs. Yours sincerely: Use 'Yours faithfully' when the salutation is 'Sir/Madam' (you don't know the receiver's name). Use 'Yours sincerely' when the salutation includes the receiver's name (e.g., 'Dear Mr. Sharma'). This distinction is strictly tested in NEB exams and is a common source of mark deductions.

Subject line in formal letters: A formal letter must have a subject line ('Subject: ...') that concisely states the purpose. An informal letter never has a subject line. Forgetting the subject line in a formal letter is a frequent error that costs marks.

Date placement: In formal letters, the date goes below the sender's address. In informal letters, the date can go below the sender's address or at the top right. The key is consistency — the date should never appear before the sender's address in any letter format.

Salutation in formal letters: 'Dear Sir/Madam' is used when the name is unknown. 'Dear Mr./Ms. [Name]' is used when the name is known. Never use 'Dear Sir' alone in modern formal writing — 'Dear Sir/Madam' is more inclusive and appropriate. In informal letters, use 'Dear [First Name],' followed by a comma.

Informal letter closing: Informal letter closings vary by relationship: 'Love' (close family), 'Your friend' (friend), 'Your loving [relation]' (elder relative), 'Best wishes' (acquaintance). Formal closings are fixed: 'Yours faithfully' or 'Yours sincerely'. Confusing these closing formulas is a common error.
practice: Write the correct closing for a formal letter to the Editor of The Kathmandu Post. [Answer: 'Yours faithfully' (if no name given) or 'Yours sincerely' (if the editor's name is known).]

Identify the error: 'Dear Sir, I am writing to complain about the poor quality of the product I purchased. Yours truly, Ram Thapa.' [Answer: 'Yours truly' is incorrect. Should be 'Yours faithfully' (formal letter with 'Dear Sir').]
Write a subject line for a formal letter complaining about irregular electricity supply in your area. [Answer: 'Subject: Complaint about irregular electricity supply in our area.']

Convert this informal sentence to formal: 'I'm writing 'cause my phone broke and I need a new one.' [Answer: 'I am writing to inform you that my mobile phone has been damaged and I require a replacement.']

Write the opening paragraph of a formal letter to the principal requesting permission to organise a cleanliness campaign. [Answer: 'I am writing to request your permission to organise a cleanliness campaign in and around our school premises on [date]. This initiative aims to promote environmental awareness among students and maintain a hygienic school environment.']
Write a subject line for a formal letter of enquiry about a scholarship programme. [Answer: 'Subject: Enquiry about scholarship programme for Class 11 students.']

Identify the type of letter required: 'Write a letter to your friend inviting him to spend the Dashain holiday with you in your village.' [Answer: Informal letter — writing to a friend about a personal invitation.] — Note the keywords: 'friend', 'Dashain holiday', 'village' all indicate informal context.

What is wrong with this informal letter closing? 'Give my regards to everybody. Yours sincerely, Sita.' [Answer: 'Yours sincerely' is a formal closing. For an informal letter to a friend, use 'Your friend' or 'Love' instead.] — This is a classic NEB exam error.

Write the correct salutation for a formal letter when the receiver's name is unknown. [Answer: 'Dear Sir/Madam,' — not 'Dear Sir' alone, as this is outdated and gender-exclusive.] — Note: In some NEB contexts, 'Dear Sir' is still accepted, but 'Dear Sir/Madam' is preferred.

Arrange the correct order of elements in a formal letter: (a) Date (b) Sender's address (c) Subject (d) Salutation (e) Body (f) Closing (g) Signature. [Answer: b → a → (receiver's address) → d → c → e → f → g]
universalFacts: Letter writing is one of the oldest forms of written communication, with examples dating back to ancient Mesopotamia (c. 3000 BCE) on clay tablets. The formal letter format has evolved significantly but retains core structural elements from centuries-old conventions.

In the NEB English examination, letter writing typically carries 8-12 marks, making it one of the highest-weighted writing tasks. Students who master both formal and informal letter formats are well-positioned to score highly in the writing section.

The distinction between 'Yours faithfully' and 'Yours sincerely' is a hallmark of British English letter-writing conventions, which the NEB syllabus follows. American English tends to use 'Sincerely' or 'Sincerely yours' for all formal letters, regardless of whether the name is known.

Letter writing is a practical life skill that extends beyond academics. The ability to write a formal complaint, application, or enquiry letter is valuable in professional and civic contexts, making this topic relevant both for exams and for real-world communication.

In Nepali letter writing tradition (पत्र लेखन), the format differs significantly from English. Nepali letters typically begin with a religious invocation (जय कमलादेवी), use different address conventions, and follow a more hierarchical social structure in salutations. Understanding these differences helps students avoid literal translation errors.
